title: KV Store Full Architecture
description: End-to-end walkthrough of a distributed KV store: client routing, coordinator nodes, read repair, hinted handoff, Merkle tree anti-entropy, and complete failure scenario analysis.

segments.text: Let's trace a complete request through a distributed key-value store like DynamoDB or Riak. A client wants to write key 'user:42'. The journey involves five components: client library, coordinator, storage nodes, replication, and anti-entropy. Each one has failure modes that you must handle.

The client library hashes the key using consistent hashing to determine the primary node. Dynamo-style systems use a ring — the key hashes to a position, and the first N nodes clockwise from that position form the preference list. The client contacts the first node in the preference list — this becomes the coordinator.

The coordinator receives the write request and fans it out to all N replica nodes — typically three. With W equals two, it waits for two successful acknowledgments before responding to the client. This gives you tunable consistency: W equals one is fast but risky, W equals N is safe but slow, W equals majority is the sweet spot.

On read with R equals two, the coordinator queries all three replicas but only waits for two responses. If the two responses have different versions — detected by vector clocks or timestamps — the coordinator returns the latest and triggers read repair on the stale node. This is eventual consistency in action.

Node C is down during a write. The coordinator can't reach it. Instead of failing, it writes a 'hint' to another node — node D. The hint says 'this data belongs to node C, forward it when C recovers.' When C comes back online, D forwards the hinted writes. This is hinted handoff — it prevents data loss during temporary failures.
What happens if node C is down for a week? The hints pile up on node D. Node D's disk fills up with other nodes' data. How would you handle long-term node failures differently from temporary ones?
segments.thought_prompt: When does hinted handoff become insufficient? What mechanism handles long-term node failures?

segments.text: Merkle trees handle long-term anti-entropy. Each node builds a hash tree over its key range. To sync, two nodes compare root hashes. If they differ, traverse down the tree to find exactly which key ranges diverge. This identifies inconsistencies by exchanging only log-N hashes instead of comparing every key — Cassandra runs this repair process periodically.

Let's enumerate failure scenarios. Single node failure: hinted handoff covers it. Network partition between replicas: sloppy quorum allows writes to continue with replacement nodes. Data corruption: Merkle trees detect and repair. Entire datacenter failure: cross-datacenter replication with asynchronous replication lag — DynamoDB Global Tables handle this.

When two writes happen to the same key on different nodes during a partition, you have a conflict. Last-write-wins uses timestamps — simple but loses data. Vector clocks detect concurrent writes and let the application resolve conflicts. Amazon's shopping cart famously used 'merge all items' as its conflict resolution — better to show a deleted item than lose a purchase.

You're building a KV store for session data — one hundred million users, five-kilobyte sessions, ninety-ninth percentile read latency under five milliseconds. What replication factor, quorum settings, and conflict resolution strategy would you choose?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a KV store for 100M user sessions with sub-5ms p99 reads. What are your N, R, W settings?

segments.text: A distributed KV store is layers of failure handling. Consistent hashing for routing, tunable quorums for consistency, hinted handoff for temporary failures, Merkle trees for long-term repair, and conflict resolution for concurrent writes. Each layer addresses a specific failure mode. Understanding these layers is what separates a textbook answer from a Staff-level design.
